text: Every programmer, at every level, spends a large share of their time looking at error messages. The difference between a beginner and an experienced analyst isn't that the experienced one sees fewer errors — it's that they read them calmly, know what the common ones mean, and have a routine for tracking down the cause. This lesson gives you that routine and finishes Chapter 1.

When Python hits an error, it stops and prints a traceback — the chain of calls that led to the failure. Here, avg underscore order divides a sum by a length. Call report on two customers, and Python prints Ada's average before failing on Grace, who has an empty order list, with a ZeroDivisionError. Read a traceback from the bottom up: the last line names the error type and the reason. The entries above it are the path Python took to get there, most recent call last. Here, Grace's empty list means len of totals is zero.

Most errors you'll meet fall into a handful of types. A KeyError means a dictionary key doesn't exist. A TypeError means the wrong type for an operation — like adding a string to a number. A ValueError means the right type but an unusable value, such as trying to convert the text n-slash-a into a float. A NameError usually means a typo, or in a notebook, a cell you forgot to run. You'll also run into IndexError for a position past the end of a list, and AttributeError when a method doesn't exist on that type.

Sometimes an error isn't a bug — it's a fact of messy data. A column of prices might contain the text n-slash-a or a blank string. Wrap the risky step in try, and catch only the specific error you expect — here, ValueError. Loop over a list of raw strings, try converting each to a float, and on failure print which value got skipped using repr, so empty strings and stray spaces become visible. The clean result keeps only the numbers that actually converted. Catch a specific exception, never a bare except, which hides real bugs.

You can raise an error deliberately when your function receives input it can't handle. Define safe underscore avg to raise a ValueError with a clear message, no orders to average, when the list is empty — instead of a mysterious division error. An assertion is a one-line sanity check that stays silent when true and raises an AssertionError when false. Assert that safe underscore avg of 10 and 20 equals 15, and it passes silently; assert it equals 20, and it raises. Assertions state what you believe about your data, and become the seed of real testing in Chapter 7.

Here's a routine that works every time. Read the last line of the traceback first — it names the problem. Then find your own line by working up through the traceback to your code, not the library's. Inspect the values: add a print of repr of x and type of x right before the failing line — guessing what a variable holds is the most common way to waste an hour. Then shrink the problem, reducing the data to the smallest input that still fails. Use a debugger when printing isn't enough — Python's built-in breakpoint function pauses execution so you can look around. Fix it, then rerun from a clean state with Restart Kernel and Run All.

To recap: read tracebacks bottom-up, error type and reason first, then your own line. Learn the common exceptions — KeyError, TypeError, ValueError, NameError, and friends. Use try and except for expected data problems, raise for invalid input, and assert for sanity checks. Next lesson starts Chapter 2, NumPy, with arrays and vectorization.
